title: Le passé composé / The past perfect
bridge: The passé composé is the equivalent of the present perfect in Spanish ('he comido', 'has ido'). In French, it is formed with an auxiliary (avoir or être) conjugated in the present tense + the past participle of the verb. The key is knowing which verbs use être and which use avoir.
rule:
FORMATION: auxiliary (avoir/être) in present tense + past participle.

AUXILIARY AVOIR (majority of verbs):
- j'ai parlé, tu as mangé, il/elle a fini, nous avons pris, vous avez vu, ils/elles ont fait

AUXILIARY ÊTRE (verbs of movement/state + all reflexive verbs):
DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP: Devenir, Revenir, Monter, Rester, Sortir, Venir, Aller, Naître, Descendre, Entrer, Rentrer, Tomber, Retourner, Arriver, Mourir, Partir
- With être, the participle agrees in gender and number with the subject:
  Il est allé / Elle est allée / Ils sont allés / Elles sont allées

COMMON IRREGULAR PAST PARTICIPLES:
- avoir → eu | être → été | faire → fait | prendre → pris | voir → vu | venir → venu | pouvoir → pu | vouloir → voulu | savoir → su | boire → bu | lire → lu | écrire → écrit | dire → dit | mettre → mis | ouvrir → ouvert | recevoir → reçu

title: Être en train de + infinitif
bridge: To express an action in progress (equivalent to Spanish 'estar + gerundio': 'estoy comiendo', 'está trabajando'), French uses the construction 'être en train de + infinitive'. The French gerund exists but has another use; this structure is the exact equivalent of the Spanish progressive.
rule:
FORMATION: être (conjugated) + en train de + infinitive

Conjugation of être in the present tense:
- je suis / tu es / il-elle est / nous sommes / vous êtes / ils-elles sont

Examples:
- Je suis en train de manger. (I am eating.)
- Il est en train de travailler. (He is working.)
- Nous sommes en train de regarder un film. (We are watching a movie.)

NOTE: Before a vowel or silent h, 'de' contracts: 'en train d'apprendre', 'en train d'habiller'.

USE: It is used to emphasize that the action is happening exactly at that moment. Without this construction, the simple present also expresses habitual actions; 'être en train de' specifies the current instant.

concept_examples.text: Je suis en train de lire.
concept_examples.translation: I am reading (right now).

concept_examples.text: Elle est en train de cuisiner.
concept_examples.translation: She is cooking.

concept_examples.text: Nous sommes en train d'apprendre le français.
concept_examples.translation: We are learning French.
concept_examples.phonetic: /nu sɔm ɑ̃ tʁɛ̃ dapʁɑ̃dʁ lə fʁɑ̃sɛ/

concept_examples.text: Ils sont en train de jouer dehors.
concept_examples.translation: They are playing outside.
concept_examples.phonetic: /il sɔ̃ ɑ̃ tʁɛ̃ də ʒwe dəɔʁ/

common_error.correct: Je suis en train de manger.
common_error.correct_alt: Je mange. (in context where it is understood)
common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers try to copy the Spanish 'estoy comiendo' using the French present participle (mangeant) with être, but that construction does not exist in French to express the progressive. The correct form is 'être en train de + infinitive'. The gerund 'en mangeant' exists but means 'while I eat / when eating'.

title: Le futur proche / Near Future
bridge: The futur proche is equivalent to the Spanish 'ir a + infinitive' ('voy a comer', 'vas a salir'). It is used to talk about immediate plans or short-term intentions. In French, it is formed with the verb 'aller' conjugated in the present tense + infinitive, exactly as in Spanish.
rule:
FORMATION: aller (present) + infinitive

Conjugation of aller in the present tense:
- je vais / tu vas / il-elle va / nous allons / vous allez / ils-elles vont

Examples:
- Je vais manger. (I am going to eat.)
- Tu vas partir ? (Are you going to leave?)
- Il va pleuvoir. (It is going to rain.)
- Nous allons voyager. (We are going to travel.)
- Vous allez comprendre. (You are going to understand.)
- Ils vont arriver bientôt. (They are going to arrive soon.)

NEGATION: ne + aller + pas + infinitive
- Je ne vais pas sortir. (I am not going to go out.)
- Il ne va pas comprendre. (He is not going to understand.)

USAGE vs FUTUR SIMPLE: The futur proche expresses concrete plans and immediate intentions. The futur simple expresses more distant or hypothetical predictions.

concept_examples.text: Je vais appeler ma mère.
concept_examples.translation: I am going to call my mother.

concept_examples.text: Nous allons visiter le musée.
concept_examples.translation: We are going to visit the museum.

concept_examples.text: Il va faire beau demain.
concept_examples.translation: It is going to be nice weather tomorrow.

concept_examples.text: Elles ne vont pas venir.
concept_examples.translation: They are not going to come.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'voy a comer' includes the preposition 'a' because 'ir' requires that preposition. In French, 'aller' in the futur proche is directly followed by the infinitive without any preposition. The 'à' only appears when 'aller' indicates movement toward a place ('Je vais à Paris'), not when it forms the near future.

examples.note: Immediate plan; je vais + infinitive

examples.original: Tu vas regarder la télé ?

title: Le futur simple / The simple future
bridge: The simple future expresses more distant future actions or predictions. In Spanish it is equivalent to the simple future ('comeré', 'vivirás', 'irá'). Unlike Spanish, in French it is formed by adding endings directly to the infinitive of the verb (without separating it), which makes it very regular. The endings are identical for all groups.
rule:
FORMATION: infinitive + endings

ENDINGS (same for all verbs):
-ai / -as / -a / -ons / -ez / -ont

-ER and -IR VERBS: they are added to the full infinitive
- parler → je parlerai, tu parleras, il parlera, nous parlerons, vous parlerez, ils parleront
- finir → je finirai, tu finiras, il finira...

-RE VERBS: the final -e is removed before adding the endings
- prendre → je prendrai, tu prendras...
- vendre → je vendrai...

IMPORTANT IRREGULARS (irregular stem, same endings):
- être → ser-: je serai, tu seras...
- avoir → aur-: j'aurai, tu auras...
- aller → ir-: j'irai, tu iras...
- faire → fer-: je ferai, tu feras...
- venir → viendr-: je viendrai...
- voir → verr-: je verrai...
- pouvoir → pourr-: je pourrai...
- vouloir → voudr-: je voudrai...
- savoir → saur-: je saurai...
- devoir → devr-: je devrai...

concept_examples.text: Je parlerai français couramment.
concept_examples.translation: I will speak French fluently.

concept_examples.text: Nous serons en retard.
concept_examples.translation: We will be late.

common_error.explanation: The futur proche (aller + infinitive) is not combined with the futur simple. They are two alternative structures: either you use 'je vais parler' (near future) or you use 'je parlerai' (simple future), never both together. The simple future is formed directly on the infinitive plus the endings.

title: Les comparatifs et superlatifs / Comparatives and Superlatives
bridge: Comparisons in French are very similar to Spanish. To compare, we use 'plus' (more), 'moins' (less), and 'aussi' (as...as), followed by the adjective and the particle 'que'. For the superlative, the definite article (le/la/les) is added before plus/moins. There are two important irregulars: bon → meilleur and mauvais → pire.
rule:
COMPARATIVES:
- Superiority: plus + adjective + que → Elle est plus grande que lui. (She is taller than him.)
- Inferiority: moins + adjective + que → C'est moins cher que je pensais. (It's less expensive than I thought.)
- Equality: aussi + adjective + que → Il est aussi intelligent qu'elle. (He is as intelligent as she is.)

SUPERLATIVES:
- Superiority: le/la/les + plus + adjective (+ de) → C'est la plus belle ville du monde.
- Inferiority: le/la/les + moins + adjective (+ de) → C'est le moins cher de tous.

ADJECTIVE POSITION: follows the usual position of the adjective in French:
- Postposed adjective: la ville la plus belle (the adjective follows the noun)
- Preposed adjective: le plus grand problème (grand goes before the noun)

IRREGULARS:
- bon/bonne → meilleur/meilleure (comparative) → le meilleur / la meilleure (superlative)
  ✗ plus bon ✓ meilleur
- mauvais/mauvaise → pire (comparative) → le pire / la pire (superlative)
  ✗ plus mauvais ✓ pire (although 'plus mauvais' is also used in colloquial language)

COMPARATIVES OF ADVERBS:
- vite → plus vite que / moins vite que / aussi vite que
- bien → mieux (better) — irregular
  ✗ plus bien ✓ mieux

title: Les verbes modaux : devoir, pouvoir, vouloir, savoir
bridge: Modal verbs in French work the same way as in Spanish: they are conjugated and followed by an infinitive. 'Devoir' is equivalent to 'should/have to', 'pouvoir' to 'can', 'vouloir' to 'want', and 'savoir' to 'know how to do something'. The key difference from Spanish is that 'savoir' only expresses learned ability, while 'pouvoir' expresses possibility or permission.
rule:
PRESENT TENSE CONJUGATION:

DEVOIR (must, have to — obligation):
- je dois / tu dois / il-elle doit / nous devons / vous devez / ils-elles doivent

POUVOIR (can — ability, possibility, permission):
- je peux / tu peux / il-elle peut / nous pouvons / vous pouvez / ils-elles peuvent

VOULOIR (want — desire, intention):
- je veux / tu veux / il-elle veut / nous voulons / vous voulez / ils-elles veulent

SAVOIR (know how — acquired skill):
- je sais / tu sais / il-elle sait / nous savons / vous savez / ils-elles savent

ALL + INFINITIVE WITHOUT PREPOSITION:
- Je dois partir. / Tu peux venir. / Elle veut danser. / Il sait nager.

KEY DISTINCTION pouvoir vs savoir:
- Je sais nager. (I know how to swim — learned skill)
- Je peux nager ici. (I can swim here — I am allowed / conditions allow)

POLITE FORMS:
- Pourriez-vous m'aider ? (Could you help me?) — conditional of pouvoir
- Je voudrais un café. (I would like a coffee.) — conditional of vouloir

For circumstantial possibility or permission ('I can do something at this moment / in this situation') use 'pouvoir'. In Spanish, 'saber' and 'poder' are sometimes confused colloquially, but in French the distinction is strict.

title: Les verbes pronominaux
bridge: Pronominal (reflexive) verbs work similarly to Spanish: they carry a reflexive pronoun ('se lever' = to get up, 'se coucher' = to go to bed, 's'appeler' = to be called). The main difference is in the passé composé: in French, ALL pronominal verbs use 'être' as the auxiliary, and the past participle must agree in gender and number with the subject in most cases.
rule:
PRESENT TENSE CONJUGATION (example: se lever — to get up):
- je me lève / tu te lèves / il-elle se lève / nous nous levons / vous vous levez / ils-elles se lèvent

REFLEXIVE PRONOUNS:
- me (m') / te (t') / se (s') / nous / vous / se (s')
Before a vowel or silent h: me → m', te → t', se → s'

COMMON PRONOMINAL VERBS:
- se lever (to get up) | se coucher (to go to bed) | se réveiller (to wake up)
- se laver (to wash) | se doucher (to shower) | s'habiller (to get dressed)
- s'appeler (to be called) | se sentir (to feel) | s'ennuyer (to be bored)
- se souvenir de (to remember) | se dépêcher (to hurry) | se tromper (to be mistaken)

PASSÉ COMPOSÉ (always with être):
- Je me suis levé(e). / Tu t'es levé(e). / Il s'est levé. / Elle s'est levée.
- Nous nous sommes levé(e)s. / Vous vous êtes levé(e)(s). / Ils se sont levés. / Elles se sont levées.

PAST PARTICIPLE AGREEMENT:
- Agrees with the subject when the reflexive pronoun is the direct object (most common case).
- Does NOT agree if there is a different explicit direct object: Elle s'est lavé les mains. (les mains = DO, 's'' = IO → no agreement)

NEGATION: ne is placed before the reflexive pronoun:
- Je ne me lève pas tôt. / Il ne s'est pas rasé.

title: Les pronoms COD et COI / Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns
bridge: In French, direct object pronouns (COD) and indirect object pronouns (COI) replace the complement and are placed BEFORE the conjugated verb, unlike Spanish where they can go before or after. The COD replaces a person or thing without a preposition; the COI replaces a person introduced by 'à'. The distinction le/lui and les/leur is key: le/la/les for COD; lui/leur for COI.
rule:
COD PRONOUNS (direct object — no preposition):
- me / te / le (masc.) / la (fem.) / nous / vous / les (plural)
- Je le vois. (I see him.) | Je la connais. (I know her.) | Je les appelle. (I call them.)

COI PRONOUNS (indirect object — replace 'à + person'):
- me / te / lui (sing.) / nous / vous / leur (plural)
- Je lui parle. (I talk to him/her.) | Je leur écris. (I write to them.)

POSITION: always BEFORE the conjugated verb:
- Je le mange. / Tu lui parles. / Il nous aide.

WITH INFINITIVE: the pronoun goes before the infinitive:
- Je vais le faire. (I am going to do it.) | Tu peux lui écrire. (You can write to him/her.)

WITH PASSÉ COMPOSÉ: the pronoun goes before the auxiliary:
- Je l'ai vu. (I saw him.) | Tu lui as parlé. (You talked to him/her.)

NEGATION: ne + pronoun + verb + pas:
- Je ne le vois pas. / Il ne lui a pas répondu.

DISTINCTION le/lui:
- le = masculine singular COD (him/it) → Je le vois. (I see him.)
- lui = singular COI m/f (to him/her) → Je lui parle. (I talk to him/her.)

concept_examples.translation: I know him well.

concept_examples.text: Tu lui as téléphoné ?

concept_examples.translation: She invites them to dinner.

common_error.explanation: The verb 'parler' takes an indirect object in French: 'parler à quelqu'un'. Therefore, it is replaced with the COI 'lui' (or 'leur' in plural), never with the COD 'le/la'. Also, the pronoun always goes BEFORE the verb, not after. Spanish speakers sometimes place the pronoun after the verb by analogy with Spanish ('hablarle' as an enclitic).

title: Les adverbes de fréquence / Adverbs of Frequency
bridge: French adverbs of frequency are similar to those in Spanish ('siempre', 'a veces', 'nunca'). The main difference is their position: in French they go AFTER the conjugated verb (not at the beginning or end of the sentence as in Spanish). In compound tenses, they go between the auxiliary and the participle. 'Jamais' in negation is always used with 'ne'.
rule:
ADVERBS OF FREQUENCY (from highest to lowest):
- toujours (always) → Je travaille toujours le lundi.
- souvent (often, frequently) → Il sort souvent le soir.
- parfois / quelquefois (sometimes) → Elle mange parfois au restaurant.
- rarement (rarely, seldom) → Nous voyageons rarement.
- ne... jamais (never) → Je ne mange jamais de viande.

POSITION:
1. In present/imperfect/simple future: subject + verb + adverb
   - Elle mange souvent des pâtes.
2. In passé composé: auxiliary + adverb + participle
   - J'ai souvent visité ce musée. / Il n'a jamais mangé de sushi.
3. 'Toujours' and 'souvent' can also go at the end of the sentence for emphasis.

JAMAIS WITHOUT NEGATION:
- In interrogative or hypothetical sentences, 'jamais' can be used without 'ne' and means 'ever':
  Tu as jamais essayé le sushi ? (Have you ever tried sushi?) — colloquial register

OTHER USEFUL ADVERBS:
- encore (still, yet) | déjà (already) | ne... plus (no longer) | ne... pas encore (not yet)

Putting them at the beginning sounds very strange. In the passé composé, they must go between the auxiliary and the participle: 'J'ai souvent mangé au restaurant', not at the end.

title: Les prépositions de temps / Prepositions of time
bridge: French time prepositions can be confusing for Spanish speakers because several of them translate to 'en' or 'hace' in Spanish depending on the context. The most problematic are 'depuis' (since/for, with present or imperfect), 'il y a' (ago — elapsed time), and 'dans' (in — future time). Mastering these prepositions is essential for speaking accurately about time.
rule:
PREPOSITIONS OF TIME:

À — exact time, specific moment:
- à midi, à trois heures, à Noël, au printemps

EN — months, years, seasons (except printemps), duration:
- en janvier, en 2024, en été, en automne, en hiver
- en deux heures (in two hours — duration of the action)

DANS — future time from now, or context/moment:
- dans trois jours (in three days) | dans cinq minutes (in five minutes)

PENDANT — complete duration of an action (past, present, or future):
- pendant deux heures (for two hours) | pendant les vacances (during the holidays)

DEPUIS — action that started in the past and continues in the present:
- Je vis ici depuis cinq ans. (I have lived here for five years.) — PRESENT
- Il attendait depuis une heure. (He had been waiting for an hour.) — IMPERFECT
- Key difference from Spanish! In French: present/imperfect + depuis

IL Y A — time elapsed since something happened (past):
- Il est arrivé il y a deux heures. (He arrived two hours ago.)
- Je l'ai vu il y a une semaine. (I saw him a week ago.)

POUR — planned or intended duration:
- Je pars pour trois semaines. (I'm leaving for three weeks — planned)
- Je suis venu pour une heure. (I came for an hour.)

In French: depuis + présent = ongoing action.

title: Les conjonctions de coordination et subordination / Coordinating and Subordinating Conjunctions
bridge: Conjunctions in French are very similar to those in Spanish in function, but some have important nuances. 'Et' (and), 'mais' (but), and 'ou' (or) are straightforward. The most important thing for a Spanish speaker is to distinguish 'parce que' (because — cause) from 'donc' (therefore — consequence) and 'pourtant/cependant' (however — contrast), which in Spanish are sometimes confused.
rule:
COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS:
- et (and): J'aime le café et le thé.
- mais (but): Je veux venir, mais je suis fatigué.
- ou (or): Tu veux du pain ou des pâtes ?
- donc (therefore, so — consequence): Il pleut, donc je prends un parapluie.
- alors (then, so — consequence / in that case): Tu n'es pas là ? Alors j'attends.

SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS:
- parce que (because — expresses cause): Je reste à la maison parce qu'il pleut.
  → Before a vowel: parce qu'
- quand (when — time): Quand j'ai faim, je mange.
  ⚠️ With future: if the action is future, use future in both clauses: Quand il arrivera, nous partirons.
- si (if — condition): Si tu études, tu réussiras.
  ⚠️ si + present → future | si + imperfect → conditional

CONTRAST CONJUNCTIONS:
- pourtant (however, despite that — opposition to what was said before): C'est difficile, pourtant j'essaie.
- cependant (however, nevertheless — more formal register): Le plan est bon ; cependant, il manque des ressources.

KEY DIFFERENCE:
- parce que → Why? — answers cause: Je pleure parce que je suis triste.
- donc/alors → consequence: Je suis triste, donc je pleure.

title: Passé composé vs Imparfait
bridge: This is one of the most important distinctions in French and the one that presents the most difficulties for Spanish speakers. In Spanish, there is also a distinction between the preterite ('comí', 'llegó') and the imperfect ('comía', 'llegaba'), but in French it is more systematic and strict. The golden rule: passé composé = punctual/completed action; imparfait = state, description, habit, or ongoing action in the past.
rule:
PASSÉ COMPOSÉ — when to use it:
1. Punctual and completed action: J'ai mangé une pizza. (I ate a pizza — once, it's over.)
2. Sequence of actions: Il est entré, a enlevé son manteau et s'est assis.
3. Defined number of times: J'ai visité Paris trois fois.
4. Action that interrupts another ongoing action: Il lisait quand le téléphone a sonné.

IMPARFAIT — when to use it:
1. Description in the past (state, appearance, condition): La maison était grande et calme.
2. Habit or repeated action in the past: Quand j'étais enfant, je jouais dehors chaque soir.
3. Ongoing action that was interrupted: Je dormais quand tu as appelé.
4. Context / narrative background: Il faisait nuit et il pleuvait.

FORMATION OF THE IMPARFAIT:
- Base: stem of 'nous' in the present (e.g., nous mangeons → mange-)
- Endings: -ais / -ais / -ait / -ions / -iez / -aient
- Example: parler → je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait, nous parlions, vous parliez, ils parlaient
- ONLY IRREGULAR: être → j'étais, tu étais, il était, nous étions, vous étiez, ils étaient

MNEMONIC TRICK:
- Passé composé = photo (punctual action, can be 'photographed')
- Imparfait = film/background (context, states, ongoing actions)

TYPICAL COMBINATION:
- Imparfait (background) + passé composé (action): Je lisais quand il a sonné à la porte.

title: L'impératif / The Imperative
bridge: The imperative in French works similarly to Spanish: it is used to give orders, instructions, advice, or requests. It is conjugated in three forms: tu (you informal), nous (we), and vous (you formal/plural). The main difference from Spanish is that -ER verbs lose the final -s in the 'tu' form, and object pronouns go after the verb in the affirmative imperative (as in Spanish: '¡dímelo!'), but before it in the negative.
rule:
FORMATION:
- Use the present indicative without a subject pronoun.
- Forms: tu / nous / vous

-ER VERBS (and aller): the -s is dropped in the 'tu' form:
- parler: Parle ! / Parlons ! / Parlez !
- manger: Mange ! / Mangeons ! / Mangez !
- EXCEPTION: if followed by 'y' or 'en': Vas-y ! / Parles-en !

-IR and -RE VERBS: keep the normal forms:
- finir: Finis ! / Finissons ! / Finissez !
- prendre: Prends ! / Prenons ! / Prenez !

IMPORTANT IRREGULARS:
- être → sois / soyons / soyez (be / let's be / be)
- avoir → aie / ayons / ayez (have / let's have / have)
- savoir → sache / sachons / sachez (know / let's know / know)
- vouloir → veuille / veuillons / veuillez (only in formal use: Veuillez vous asseoir.)

NEGATIVE IMPERATIVE:
- ne + verb + pas: Ne parle pas ! / Ne mange pas ça !

PRONOUNS WITH IMPERATIVE:
Affirmative: pronoun goes AFTER the verb with a hyphen:
- Mange-le ! (Eat it!) | Dis-moi la vérité. (Tell me the truth.) | Allez-y ! (Go!)
- me/te → moi/toi after the verb: Donne-moi ça. / Assieds-toi.

Negative: pronoun goes BEFORE the verb:
- Ne le mange pas ! (Don't eat it!) | Ne me dis pas ça. (Don't tell me that.)

Many Spanish speakers add the -s by analogy with the present indicative ('tu parles') or with Spanish ('habla' has no -s, but 'comes' does → confusion). The exception: if followed by 'y' or 'en', the -s returns to avoid cacophony: 'Parles-en' (talk about it), 'Vas-y' (go there).

title: Les articles partitifs et les noms indénombrables / Partitive articles and uncountable nouns
bridge: In Spanish, there is also a distinction between what can be counted ('un libro', 'dos libros') and what cannot ('agua', 'azúcar', 'música'). However, French requires specific partitive articles (du, de la, de l', des) to express 'some', 'a part of' something, equivalent to Spanish 'un poco de' or sometimes the zero article. This system does not exist in the same way in Spanish, which leads to many omission errors.
rule:
PARTITIVE ARTICLES (express an indeterminate quantity of something):
- du (de + le, masc. sing.): Je mange du pain. (I eat bread / some bread.)
- de la (fem. sing.): Elle boit de la limonade. (She drinks lemonade.)
- de l' (before a vowel or silent h): Il boit de l'eau. / Tu veux de l'huile ?
- des (plural — countable nouns in indeterminate quantity): J'achète des fruits.

WHEN TO USE PARTITIVES:
- Uncountable nouns (mass, liquids, abstract): pain, eau, lait, musique, courage, temps
- Foods and drinks without precise quantity: Je veux du café. / Il prend de la soupe.

WHEN TO USE THE INDEFINITE ARTICLE (un/une/des):
- Countable nouns: Je mange une pomme. / Il lit un livre. / J'ai des amis.

WHEN TO USE THE DEFINITE ARTICLE (le/la/les):
- To talk about something in general or as a category: J'aime le café. (I like coffee — in general.) / Le courage est important.
- After verbs of taste (aimer, adorer, préférer, détester): J'adore la musique.

NEGATION — KEY RULE:
After negation (ne...pas), du/de la/de l'/des → de (d'):
- Je mange du pain. → Je ne mange pas de pain.
- Elle boit de la limonade. → Elle ne boit pas de limonade.
- Il a des amis. → Il n'a pas d'amis.
⚠️ EXCEPTION: with the verb être, the article does not change:
- C'est du chocolat. → Ce n'est pas du chocolat. (not → ce n'est pas de chocolat)

title: Les indéfinis : quelque(s), certain(s), plusieurs, chaque, tout/toute/tous/toutes / Indefinites: some, certain, several, each, all
bridge: In Spanish there are quantifiers and indefinites like 'algún/alguna', 'cierto/cierta', 'varios/varias', 'cada' and 'todo/toda/todos/todas'. French has direct equivalents, but with particularities: 'chaque' is invariable (no plural), 'tout' varies in gender and number, and 'quelque(s)' has a more restricted use than 'alguno' in Spanish.
rule:
QUELQUE(S) — some/any (singular), some (plural):
- Singular: quelque (rare in singular, more literary): quelque chose (something), quelque part (somewhere)
- Plural: quelques = some: J'ai quelques amis. (I have some friends.)
- Note: in everyday use 'quelques' is much more frequent than the singular.

CERTAIN(S) / CERTAINE(S) — certain, some:
- masc. sing.: certain | fem. sing.: certaine
- masc. pl.: certains | fem. pl.: certaines
- Certains étudiants travaillent beaucoup. (Certain students work a lot.)
- Dans certains cas, c'est difficile. (In certain cases, it's difficult.)

PLUSIEURS — several (invariable in gender):
- J'ai plusieurs questions. (I have several questions.)
- Ils ont plusieurs enfants. (They have several children.)
- NOTE: plusieurs is always plural, it has no singular form.

CHAQUE — each (ALWAYS singular, invariable):
- chaque jour (each day) | chaque personne (each person)
- Chaque élève a un livre. (Each student has a book.)
- NEVER: ~~chaques~~ — the plural does not exist.

TOUT / TOUTE / TOUS / TOUTES — all, every:
- tout + def. art. masc. sing.: tout le monde (everyone), tout le temps (all the time)
- toute + def. art. fem. sing.: toute la journée (all day), toute la classe (the whole class)
- tous + def. art. masc. pl.: tous les jours (every day), tous les ans (every year)
- toutes + def. art. fem. pl.: toutes les semaines (every week)
- NOTE: 'tous' only when used alone as a pronoun is the final -s pronounced: /tus/; as a determiner: /tu/.

title: Les quantificateurs de quantité : beaucoup de, trop de, assez de, peu de, un peu de / Quantifiers of quantity: beaucoup de, trop de, assez de, peu de, un peu de
bridge: In Spanish we use expressions like 'mucho/a', 'demasiado/a', 'bastante', 'poco/a', 'un poco de' that agree in gender and number with the noun. In French, these expressions of quantity are always followed by 'de' (without an article) and are INVARIABLE: they do not change according to the gender or number of the noun that follows.
rule:
FUNDAMENTAL RULE: quantity expression + DE + noun (without article)

BEAUCOUP DE — much/many:
- beaucoup de temps (a lot of time) | beaucoup de gens (many people)
- NEVER: ~~beaucoup du / beaucoup de la / beaucoup des~~

TROP DE — too much/too many:
- trop de bruit (too much noise) | trop de voitures (too many cars)
- Negative connotation: indicates excess.

ASSEZ DE — enough:
- assez de place (enough space) | assez d'argent (enough money)
- Can be positive ('enough') or negative ('not enough' in negation).

PEU DE — little/few (insufficient quantity):
- peu de temps (little time) | peu d'amis (few friends)
- Negative connotation: indicates scarcity.

UN PEU DE — a little (small but positive quantity):
- un peu de sucre (a little sugar) | un peu de patience (a little patience)
- ONLY used with uncountable or mass nouns.
- Contrast: peu de = negative (scarcity); un peu de = positive (small quantity).

IN NEGATION: ne...pas + beaucoup/assez de + noun:
- Il n'a pas beaucoup de travail. (He doesn't have much work.)
- Elle n'a pas assez d'argent. (She doesn't have enough money.)

WITH ADJECTIVES: beaucoup/trop/assez/peu stand alone (without 'de'):
- C'est trop cher. (It's too expensive.) — adjective
- Il travaille beaucoup. (He works a lot.) — adverb

title: Les propositions relatives : qui, que, où / Relative clauses: qui, que, où
bridge: Relative clauses in French work the same as in Spanish ('que', 'quien', 'donde') but with a key difference: in French you must choose between 'qui' and 'que' depending on the grammatical function of the pronoun within the relative clause. 'Qui' replaces the subject; 'que' replaces the direct object; 'où' replaces a place or a time.
rule:
QUI — relative pronoun subject (equivalent to 'que/quien' as subject):
- Replaces the subject of the relative clause (the person or thing that does the action).
- C'est l'homme qui parle. (He is the man who speaks.) → 'qui' is the subject of 'parle'
- J'ai une amie qui habite à Lyon. (I have a friend who lives in Lyon.)
- NEVER omitted: it cannot be omitted as in English ('the man who speaks' = 'the man speaks').

QUE (QU' before a vowel) — relative pronoun direct object:
- Replaces the direct object of the relative clause (the one receiving the action).
- Le livre que je lis est intéressant. (The book that I am reading is interesting.) → 'que' is the object of 'lis'
- La fille que tu connais s'appelle Marie. (The girl you know is called Marie.)
- PAST PARTICIPLE AGREEMENT: in the passé composé, the past participle agrees with 'que' if it precedes the verb:
  La robe qu'elle a achetée est belle. (The dress she bought is beautiful.) → 'achetée' agrees with 'robe' (fem.)

OÙ — relative pronoun of place or time:
- Replaces a place complement ('where') or a time complement ('when', 'in which'):
  C'est la ville où je suis né. (It is the city where I was born.)
  Le jour où je l'ai rencontré, il pleuvait. (The day I met him, it was raining.)
- Equivalent to 'dans laquelle', 'au moment où', etc., but simpler.

TRICK for QUI vs QUE:
- If immediately after the relative pronoun comes a CONJUGATED VERB → QUI (subject)
- If after the relative pronoun comes a SUBJECT (noun/pronoun) → QUE (object)

concept_examples.text: J'ai un ami qui parle trois langues.

common_error.wrong: Le livre que j'aime est sur la table. → Le livre qui j'aime...
common_error.correct: Le livre que j'aime est sur la table.
common_error.explanation: The most frequent confusion is using 'qui' when 'que' should go and vice versa. The key is to analyze the function: in 'Le livre que j'aime', the book is the OBJECT of 'j'aime' (I love the book), so 'que' is used. If instead we said 'Le livre qui est sur la table', the book is the SUBJECT of 'est', hence 'qui'. Quick trick: does an explicit subject follow the relative pronoun? → 'que'. Does a verb directly follow without a subject? → 'qui'.

examples.note: qui + direct verb; the teacher is the one who explains

examples.note: qui subject of s'appelle; reflexive verb

examples.note: qui can refer to people or things

examples.note: qu' + vowel (elision); the song is the object of 'chante'

levels.translation: Où — relative pronoun of place and time

title: Beaucoup, très, trop / Much, very, too much
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'mucho' for both quantity and intensity ('tengo mucho trabajo', 'es muy bueno'). In French, you must distinguish between 'beaucoup' (quantity) and 'très' (intensity). Also, 'trop' means 'too much', which is often confused with 'muy' when compared to Spanish. It is important to remember that 'beaucoup' is not used with adjectives and that 'très' is not used with nouns.
rule: In French, to express 'much/many' we use 'beaucoup de' before a noun (e.g., 'beaucoup de temps'). For adjectives or adverbs we use 'très' (very) (e.g., 'très intéressant'). 'Trop' means 'too much' and is used with nouns ('trop de bruit') or with adjectives/adverbs ('trop cher') to indicate excess. 'Beaucoup' is not used with adjectives; 'très' is not used with nouns. Also, 'beaucoup de' becomes 'beaucoup d'' before a vowel or silent h. In negative sentences, 'beaucoup' becomes 'pas beaucoup' (not much) and 'de' is not used.

concept_examples.text: J'ai beaucoup de livres.
concept_examples.translation: I have many books.

concept_examples.text: Il est très intelligent.
concept_examples.translation: He is very intelligent.

concept_examples.text: Elle mange trop de gâteaux.
concept_examples.translation: She eats too many cakes.

concept_examples.text: Nous avons beaucoup d'amis.
concept_examples.translation: We have many friends.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, you say 'estoy muy cansado', but 'beaucoup' is not used with adjectives. For intensity with adjectives, use 'très' (very). If you want to say 'too tired', then use 'trop'.

examples.original: Je bois beaucoup d'eau.
examples.translation: I drink a lot of water.
examples.note: Remember that 'beaucoup de' is used with uncountable nouns like 'eau'.

examples.original: Tu as beaucoup de travail.
examples.translation: You have a lot of work.
examples.note: 'Beaucoup de' is used for quantity; here 'travail' is uncountable.

examples.original: Ce film est très intéressant.
examples.translation: This film is very interesting.
examples.note: 'Très' modifies the adjective 'intéressant'.

examples.original: Elle parle très vite.
examples.translation: She speaks very fast.
examples.note: 'Très' also modifies adverbs like 'vite'.

examples.original: Il y a trop de monde ici.
examples.phonetic: /il i a tʁo də mɔ̃d isi/
examples.translation: There are too many people here.
examples.note: 'Trop de' is used with nouns to indicate excess.

examples.original: Ce gâteau est trop sucré.
examples.translation: This cake is too sweet.
examples.note: 'Trop' with an adjective indicates excess in quality.
